analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal offshore waters to oil and gas drilling and shares lease revenue with coastal states.
analysis.headline: The House Natural Resources Committee approved it 25-19 in February 2012, but the bill never received a vote on the House floor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Interior Department to hold new offshore oil and gas lease sales off Virginia, Alaska, California, and the Gulf of Mexico, and to lease large shares of any unleased federal waters with big known oil and gas deposits. It would have shortened environmental reviews for these sales and made state coastal-management review inapplicable to the California sale. It also would have paid coastal states a growing share of the revenue from new leases, and set a national goal of 3 million more barrels of oil per day by 2027.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain guaranteed lease sales and expanded access to federal waters, with faster, thinner environmental review. Coastal states gain a share of leasing revenue they could spend freely. Offshore construction and drilling services would gain work if leases developed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies and coastal states

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Interior Secretary to conduct specific lease sales: Sale 216 and 222 in the central Gulf within months of enactment, Sale 220 off Virginia within a year, the former Sale 214 in the North Aleutian Basin within a year, and a Southern California sale by mid-2014 [S3][S4].
Requires at least 50% of available unleased acreage in each planning area with the largest oil and gas resources to be offered, plus any area a state governor requests [S2][S3].
Gives coastal states 37.5% of new leasing revenues (phased in from 12.5%), usable for any purpose without further appropriation [S3][S4].

States Congress's intent that expanded energy development support American manufacturing and jobs, and directs the Secretary to encourage hiring U.S. workers and using U.S.-made equipment, though this encouragement is not a binding requirement [S3][S4].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury loses revenue as new leasing money is redirected to coastal states. Coastal communities and ocean users bear environmental risk: new drilling off Virginia, Alaska, and Southern California with reduced environmental analysis. For the California sale, the bill deems old environmental documents sufficient for the Gulf sales, limits the environmental study to one alternative, and allows only comments filed within 20 days on the preferred action.

drawbacks.text: For the Gulf lease sales, the bill deems environmental impact statements written in 2007 and 2008 to satisfy the National Environmental Policy Act, avoiding any new environmental analysis for those sales [S3][S4].

For the Southern California sale, the Secretary would not have to analyze a non-leasing alternative, could study only one alternative besides the preferred plan, and would consider only public comments that address the preferred action and are filed within 20 days [S3][S4].
The Coastal Zone Management Act's requirement that federal activities be consistent with state coastal programs would not apply to the California lease sales and any resulting drilling [S3][S4].
Redirecting 37.5% of new leasing revenues to coastal states reduces the money flowing to the federal Treasury that otherwise funds general programs [S3][S4].

The bill's central trade-off: even the bill's supporters concede that expanded drilling carries spill and habitat risk in areas including the fisheries-rich North Aleutian Basin, and its production goals would not be met until 2027, well beyond the leasing program's five-year window [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward expansion of oil and gas access on public waters, with the environmental-review shortcuts and the 20-day comment window doing the most damage to ordinary oversight. The revenue-sharing and jobs provisions are real but smaller: revenue sharing helps coastal state budgets while draining federal receipts, and the worker-and-equipment language is an expression of intent, not an enforceable requirement. On balance the benefits flow mainly to the oil and gas industry, while the risks and reduced federal revenue fall on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The House Natural Resources Committee reported the bill to the floor in February 2012 and it was placed on the House calendar, but it never came up for a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Stivers (R-OH) introduced the bill on November 14, 2011, and it was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee [S1][S6].
On February 1, 2012, the committee ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 25-19, and the committee formally reported it on February 9, 2012 [S6].
The bill was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting House floor action, but no vote was ever scheduled, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S6][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no new lease sales were mandated off Virginia, Southern California, or the North Aleutian Basin, and the shortened environmental reviews and reduced federal revenue share never took effect. Coastal areas kept their existing protections; the oil and gas industry gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil industry gained nothing; coastal waters stayed closed

for.name: Rep. Steve Stivers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 14, 2011, and recruited the additional cosponsors who joined in February 2012.

for.name: 18 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat signed on.

for.name: House Natural Resources Committee majority
for.role: Committee with jurisdiction over offshore leasing
for.what_they_did: Discharged the subcommittee, held a markup, and voted 25-19 on February 1, 2012 to order the bill reported as amended.

against.name: 19 members of the House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Voted against ordering the bill reported when the committee marked it up on February 1, 2012.

against.name: Obama administration
against.role: Executive branch, Department of the Interior
against.what_they_did: Pursued a 2012-2017 offshore leasing plan that kept most newly prospective areas off the leasing table, putting it in conflict with the bill's mandated sales.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Republicans, and the committee's 25-19 vote to report the bill was narrow, consistent with members splitting on party lines.

industries.note: The bill would have mandated lease sales and opened at least half of the unleased acreage in the most resource-rich federal planning areas, while deeming decade-old environmental studies sufficient for Gulf sales and cutting the California sale's review to one alternative and a 20-day comment window. The industry's access expands at the cost of the environmental review and state coastal review that protect the public.

States within 200 miles of new leases would receive up to 37.5% of the leasing revenues, spendable for any purpose without appropriation. This is a real fiscal benefit to state budgets, though it comes from revenue that would otherwise go to the federal Treasury.

More mandated lease sales mean more exploration and development work, and the bill urges hiring U.S. workers and using U.S.-made equipment, though only as encouragement. Gains are contingent on leases actually being developed, which takes years.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing, tourism, and coastal businesses
industries.note: New drilling off Virginia, the North Aleutian Basin, and Southern California would introduce spill and industrial-activity risk to waters these businesses depend on, and the bill would have removed California's state coastal-zone review of the sale.
